messages.subject_clean: Method for getting model output into table?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been using INLA for some time now, and have been manually moving the output from R into tables as necessary, but I was wondering if anyone had an easier way of doing this.  I've tried using a few of the more common approaches to reading out regression, etc. outputs such as Stargazer and R2HTML but none of them seem to support INLA formatting.

How does everyone else do this?  Do they just do this by hand every time?  It was fine, but tedious, the first few times, but as I keep refining and rerunning models, it's been taking a lot of time to do it manually.  Any ideas would be appreciated.

-Jesse

The stable package is quite nice for this.
It operates mainly on data.frame:s but also knows about e.g. almost and anova output; for inla, first extract the desired columns of output, or craft a custom data.frame of the output, and then call
xtable(mydata)
and then copy-paste into your latex file.

(This is particularly useful within knitr documents, since then all that's needed to get it into the latex properly is a results='asis' chunk option.)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Stacking meshes
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Stacking meshes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalie,

you didn't specify what your model for each year is; for domains with
shifting boundary, there is no easy way of constructing a space-time
model with dependence between the time points. (If the domain is not
shifting, you could simply use a common mesh for all time points, so
I'll assume your boundaries are shifting).  So that seems to imply you
want independent fields for each time point, and only the covariates
will connect the model through time.

(Your text contradicts your code; I assume the A2 matrix should use
mesh2 and coords2 in inla.spde.make.A ? )
(Also: You say you have 10 years, but then only want 9 meshes ? )

Given the assumptions above, there are two cases:
1) You want common covariance parameters for all the years
2) You want different covariance parameters for each year.

Case 2) is tedious but easy:
Treat each year-field as a separate component,
  formula <-  covar + f(field1, model = spde1) + f(field2, model = spde2) + ...
  spde1 <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh1, ...)
  A1 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh1, loc = coords1)
  idx1 <- inla.spde.make.index("field1", n.spde = spde1$n.spde)
  stack1 <- inla.stack(
     data = list(y = y[1:1609]),
     A = list(A1, Diagonal(nrow(A1), 1.0)),
     effects = list(idx1, list(covar = covar[1:nrow(A1), 1:10, drop=FALSE]))
     )
  spde2 <- ...
  idx2 <- ...
  stack2 <- ...
  ...
  stack.total <- inla.stack(stack1, stack2, ...)

Case 1) requires a bit more work.
There is currently no tool for constructing a "join" of spde models
(one can extract the required information and do it for specific
cases,
but its non-trivial to generalise), so using just the standard
interface one solution is instead to shift each mesh so that the
combined mesh has 10 (one for each year) non-overlapping regions.
inla.spde2.pcmatern() will then construct a joint model using the same
parameters for each region.  But that shifts the problem to joining
the shifted meshes.  The easiest way to do that depends on how you
construct the meshes in the first place.
If they are all based on inla.nonconvex.hull() or shape file
boundaries, simply pre-shift the boundaries before constructing the
mesh.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Just to be clear: I unfortunately described case 2 first and then case
1, so I'll use less ambiguous terminology now:

Independent fields, separate parameters (was: case 2) is tedious but
easy to set up,
  but expensive to compute (due to the large number of field
parameters; 2 x years

Independent fields, common parameters (was: case 1) requires a bit of
work to set up,
  but is cheap(er) to compute (only 2 field parameters in total)

Dependent fields: requires either
  common mesh for all years, or
  spacial construction based on some model designed specifically for
this time-shifting domain.

In the two independent field approaches, the GMRF parts of the model
are roughly equivalent to compute,
but having separate parameters massively inflates the size of the
hyperparameter optimisation dimension.

Finn

On Thu, 2017-07-06 at 10:12 -0700, Mike wrote:
> Hello everybody,
>
> I read in this post https://goo.gl/16sJJ2  that mode$mode.status==0
> its OK, larger values are still useful, but that mode.status==1000
> means: Hessian is not SPD.
>
> My focus is on predictions and I got 1000 for my best significant
> model that includes just the spatial random effect.
>
> What does this mean?
>
> Does this means that the stochastic partial differential equation
> approach is not suitable when using just the spatial component and I
> have to select the best significant model with mode.status==1000?

it simply means that the found hessian at the mode has the wrong sign.
this can be due to two things. 1: the mode is not found sufficiently
accurate enough, or 2: the numerical approximation for the hessian
fail.

you may try to restart in these cases, like
r = inla.rerun(r)

this is the most likely reason. moreover, this usually happens when the
log posterior is almost flat, hence its back the model that is not very
informative wrt some or one of the parameters. more informative priors
would help.

Best
H

messages.subject_clean: Multiple likelihoods for mesh models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am interested in modeling two responses, (i.e. wasting and maternal overweight and obese). I have tried reading on ways to manipulate more than one likelihood but i cant seem to get a feel on the way i would go about it.

Below is a code where i fitted only one response, but wondering how i would add the other response.

##--- Constructing the SPDE object
#Assumptions: Non Stationarity and Anisotropy

basis.T <-inla.mesh.basis(mesh, type="b.spline", n=2, degree=2)
basis.K <-inla.mesh.basis(mesh, type="b.spline", n=2,degree=2)

spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
                         alpha = 2,
                         B.tau = cbind(0, basis.T, basis.K*0),
                         B.kappa = cbind(0, basis.T*0, basis.K/2))

no.years <- length(unique(data.train$time))

#names.zzz <- "the covariates in my model"

# restructure my data

n = dim(data.train)[1]
N = 2*n

##two reponses am interested in modeling
y1 <- data.train$wasting
y2 <- data.train$maternal_overweight_obese

## Join them together
Y = matrix(NA, N, 2)
Y[1:n, 1] = y1
Y[1:n + n, 2] = y2

x = data.train[,names.zzz]

##--- Observation structure for estimation data
A.est =
  inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
                   loc=
                     as.matrix(coordinates.train[data.train$cluster_id,
                                                 c("long","lat")]),
                   group = data.train$time,
                   n.group = no.years
  )

##--- Observation structure for validation data
A.val =
  inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
                   loc=
                     as.matrix(coordinates.val[data.val$cluster_id,
                                               c("long","lat")]),
                   group = data.val$time,
                   n.group = no.years
  )

i_year <- 3 #prediction year

##--- Observation structure for field prediction
A.pred =
  inla.spde.make.A(mesh ,group = i_year, n.group = no.years
  )

field.indices =
  inla.spde.make.index("field",
                       n.spde = mesh$n,
                       n.group=no.years
  )

stack.est =
  inla.stack(data=list(y = data.train$y),
             A=list(A.est, 1),
             effects=
               list(c(field.indices,
                      list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(data.train[,names.zzz])),
             tag="est")

stack.val =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),
             A=list(A.val, 1),
             effects=
               list(c(field.indices,
                      list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(data.val[,names.zzz])),
             tag="val")

scaled.mesh.loc =
  list(long=(rep(scale(mesh$loc[,1],
                       mean.covariates["long"],
                       sd.covariates["long"]),
                 no.years
  )),
  lat=(rep(scale(mesh$loc[,2],
                 mean.covariates["lat"],
                 sd.covariates["lat"]),
           no.years
  )))

stack.pred =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),
             A=list(A.pred),
             effects=
               list(c(field.indices,
                      scaled.mesh.loc,
                      list(Intercept=1))),
             tag="pred")

stack = inla.stack(stack.est, stack.val, stack.pred)
str(stack)

ntrials = c(df.final.03.train1$N,data.val$N,rep(NA,mesh$n))

#
results =
  inla(formula = f,
       data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde = spde),
       family = "binomial",
       Ntrials = ntrials,
       control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack),link = 1,compute=TRUE),
       control.compute = list(cpo=T,dic=TRUE),
       keep = FALSE,
       verbose = TRUE)

Thanks for your help.

Thomas.

The main issue is that you are not building the data stack accounting
for multiple likelihood. You can follow examples in the last Chapter of
the INLA book or in Chapter 3 of the current spde-tutorial version.

In advance you have to specify two columns data as something like this

stack.est1 = inla.stack(
data = list(y=cbind(data.train$wasting,NA),trials=data.train$N),
...)
stack.est2 = inla.stack(
data =
list(y=cbind(NA,data.train$maternal_overweight_obese),trials=data.train$N),
...)

So you have one stack for each outcome with the first in the first
column of data and the second in the second along with the number of
trials. These two data stack need to be join to use in inla().

Elias

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

First, please note that while one would _like_ these constraints to
"correct for" spatial confounding, in practice they don't necessarily
do that.  They can sometimes _help_, but you still need to be careful
about over-interpreting estimated coefficients.

That said, the extraconstr constraints in inla.spde.(pc)matern operate
on the spatial domain only, which when combined with a "group" model
such as ar1 means that it applies to each time point individually,
which is very different to applying it to the temporal average field,
for example.

Only the "iid" replication model has a workaround for this, by
constructing the replication and any associated constraints in
inla.spde2.matern itself (using n.iid.group, and not using "group" in
f() at all), which allows more general constraints on the full model.

A possibly better and more general alternative is to _not_ impose
constraints in the model, but instead choose more carefully how to
interpret the output, by computing appropriate contrasts. (A bit messy
in R-INLA itself; a bit easier in our http://inlabru.org/ package
(still in development but most things related to this already works))

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I meant that one _must_ be careful; I did not mean that there is
always and necessarily a good way of doing it.

What you describe can give indications of influence, yes, but due to
posterior correlations it's not always clear.
In the case of a spatial covariate that is reasonably smooth, it will
be confounded with a spatial field term.
Ideally, one would then like the linear covariate effect to capture
all linear effect, and the field only be substantially
non-zero if required, but that requires the parameter priors for the
field component to be chosen appropriately.
Make sure to use inla.spde2.pcmatern, since the PC-prior was developed
to help with this.

I don't understand the last part of your question in a Bayesian
hierarchical model framework,
 with a sum of a linear covariate effect and a random field component.
You seem to be talking about
a physical process through which the covariate has an effect.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Just to report back. Running the single large model on my 8 core, 16GB desktop took nearly 2 weeks. Running a non-optimised INLA on a 24 core, 128 GB server, INLA made use of 101GB of memory, running on all cores and did the job in 23 hrs. By splitting the model into a Poisson model and a binomial model then combining the outputs I could run on my desktop in 4 days - but have the disadvantage that 95% confidence intervals don't combine (obviously the joint probability of being at the 95% upper end of the Poisson model AND the 95% upper end of the binomial are not the combined model 95% quantile), which complicates things. In this example, (and as expected) the single zip model and the two models combined were more or less equivalent.

Thanks for assistance - notching this up as a success!

Colin

PS In case anyone keeps note, a couple of recent papers using INLA from my colleagues:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecog.03098/abstract

n.data=27*12  #27 sites and 12 years
X = cbind(Intercept=rep(1,n.data),temp=maxtemp, lal=lats)  #lat-latitudes of sites
Q = qr.Q(qr(X))
n.covariates=3

A.est = inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
       loc = as.matrix(obsloc))  #obsloc - latitudes and longitudes with necessary repeats

field.indices =
       inla.spde.make.index("field", n.spde=mesh$n)

spde = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh=mesh, constr=T,
       n.iid.group = yrs,           #yrs =12
       prior.range=c(0.01,0.1), prior.sigma=c(100,0.1),
       extraconstr = list(A = as.matrix(t(Q)%*%A.est), e= rep(0, n.covariates))
)

stack.est1 = inla.stack(data=list(y=l2,e=ll),                 #e-offset
       A=list(A.est, 1),
       effects= list(c(field.indices,list(Intercept=1)),
             list(temp=maxtemp, lat=lats,pop=pop, pop2=pop2)),
       tag="est")

f4 <- (y ~ -1 + Intercept + temp+ lat+f(pop,model="iid")+  #pop -site index
      f(pop2, temp, model="iid") +
      f(field, model=spde))

mod4b = inla(f4,
       data=inla.stack.data(stack.est1, spde=spde),
       family="nbinomial",E=e,

messages.body_plain:
Your code, if it runs without error (which I don't think it will),
seems to construct a constraint for each timepoint, but then averages
that constraint over all timepoints. I suspect that what you're after
is rather a constraint against the observation locations in
space-time.
(If you want an AR model in time, this method doesn't work, so I'll
assume that you're happy with a temporal iid model)

You need to change the order of the code, and modify/add some parameters:

A.est = inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
       loc = as.matrix(obsloc), group=obsyear, n.group=yrs)

spde = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh=mesh, constr=T,
       n.iid.group = yrs,           #yrs =12
       prior.range=c(0.01,0.1), prior.sigma=c(100,0.1),
       extraconstr = list(A = as.matrix(t(Q)%*%A.est), e= rep(0, n.covariates))
)

field.indices =
       inla.spde.make.index("field", n.spde=spde$n.spde)

(You should always use spde$n.spde in inla.spde.make.index. It doesn't
usually matter, but in this case it's essential, since
  n.spde will be mesh$n * yrs)

Finn

Is there a way where such a model can be constructed in INLA? I see, for example, that inla.spde.make.index() supports "replicates" but I can't quite tell if they are relevant in this case...

Cheers,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
I am not sure if your use of zeroinflatedpoisson0 is correct.

Usually for Hurdle models: Where there are 0's the "poisson-part" has an NA observation. The reasoning is that you do not know what it would have been if it had made the "hurdle" of crossing zero.

So I believe you should exchange your zeroinflatedpoisson for a poisson, or a poisson where the zeroes are removed.

PS. You could end up with similar results through different approaches, but estimating the zero-probability will get you in trouble if you have "NA and positive data".

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

It would either be:

family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0"

for a Poisson hurdle model (which means that the binary part is modelled as a function of an intercept...with no covariates..and the count part as a function of covariates).....or

family=c(’binomial’, ’zerotruncatedPoisson’)

zerotruncatedPoisson will not work. Hence......I am not sure how you can put covariates in the binary part of the model.

There are examples in the INLA literature in which this is done for continuous data (rainfall)....but in that example a gamma distribution is used for the non-zero data...and the gamma distribution is already zero truncated. So..there is works.

It would be nice if the zero truncated Poisson/NB distributions could be added to INLA....or if someone can tell me that I am wrong.
